text:
The most powerful refutation is that the felicific calculus falsely assumes pleasures and pains are commensurable on a single quantitative scale, when in reality they differ irreducibly in kind, quality, and meaning. This objection, pressed by Mill and later by critics of crude utilitarianism, shows that Bentham’s method cannot capture what actually makes lives go well or badly. Consequently, the calculus is not merely impractical but conceptually incoherent as a measure of well-being.

CONFIDENCE: 92
